decks.title: Area and Perimeter: Part 1, circumference, pi, arcs, Heron and medians
goals: Find perimeters, circumferences and arc lengths, stating the value of pi used
Describe how people approximated pi in Egypt, Greece, India and China
Use Heron's formula for the area of a triangle
Explain why a median bisects the area of a triangle

slides.heading: The way round a circle
slides.body_md: The distance round a circle is its **circumference**. For every circle it is **$\pi$ times the diameter**: $C = \pi d = 2\pi r$.

visual.alt: A circle with a diameter AB of 14 centimetres drawn through the centre O. Walking once round the circle covers 22 sevenths of the diameter, which is 44 centimetres.
visual.caption: Circumference $= \pi d = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = 44$ cm.

slides.narration: How far is it once round a bicycle wheel, a coin or a well? That distance is the circumference. If you divide the circumference by the diameter, you always get the same number, whatever the size of the circle. That number is called pi, and in this chapter we meet its long history, and use it to measure curves and areas.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Explain why a **median bisects the area**

visual.alt: Flow of Part 1: perimeter and circumference, approximations of pi through history, arc length, Heron's formula and the fact that a median bisects the area of a triangle.
visual.caption: Part 1 road map.

slides.narration: In this part we find perimeters and circumferences, and we look at how people in Egypt, Greece, India and China approximated pi. Then we find lengths of arcs. After that we learn Heron's formula, which gives the area of a triangle from its three sides, and we see why a median cuts a triangle into two equal areas.

slides.heading: Perimeter and circumference
slides.body_md: Always say which value of $\pi$ you use: $\dfrac{22}{7}$ or $3.14$. Both are only **approximations**.

visual.alt: Table of perimeters: a rectangle 2 times length plus width, a square 4 times the side, a triangle the sum of its sides, and a circle 2 pi r, which is pi times the diameter. Examples give 40, 36, 36 and 44 centimetres.
visual.caption: The distance round a circle is called its circumference. State the value of $\pi$ you use.

slides.narration: The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. For a rectangle it is twice the length plus the width. For a square it is four times the side. For a triangle, add the three sides. For a circle it is called the circumference, and it is two pi r. Always say which value of pi you are using.

slides.heading: Ancient Egypt: a square for a circle
slides.body_md: The Egyptians took the area of a circle of diameter $9$ to be the area of a square of side $8$. Then $64 = \pi \times \left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right)^2$ gives $\pi \approx \dfrac{256}{81} = \left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right)^2 \approx 3.16$.

visual.alt: A circle of diameter 9 units and a square of side 8 units, drawn on the same centre. The ancient Egyptian rule says that the two have nearly the same area: the square has area 64 and the circle has area about 63.6.
visual.caption: A square of side $\tfrac{8}{9}$ of the diameter has area $64$ for a circle of diameter $9$ (area about $63.6$).

slides.narration: Here is a rule written on an Egyptian papyrus about three and a half thousand years ago. Take a circle of diameter nine. Its area is nearly the same as the area of a square of side eight, which is sixty-four. Working backwards, this rule treats pi as two hundred fifty-six divided by eighty-one, which is about three point one six.

slides.heading: Approximations of pi through history
slides.body_md: The value of $\pi$ is $3.14159265\ldots$ No fraction equals it exactly. Later still, an **infinite series found in Kerala** gave many more decimal places.

rows: Area of a circle taken as the area of a square of side $\frac{8}{9}$ of the diameter
Trapped $\pi$ between the perimeters of polygons of $96$ sides
Gave $62832$ as the approximate circumference of a circle of diameter $20000$
A fraction often credited to Zu Chongzhi (China, 5th century CE)
Easy to use; it is also the upper bound of Archimedes

visual.alt: Table of approximations of pi: ancient Egypt about 3.1605, Archimedes between 3.1408 and 3.1429, Aryabhata 3.1416, a fraction 355 over 113 often credited to Zu Chongzhi about 3.14159, and the school value 22 over 7 about 3.1429.
visual.caption: Approximations of $\pi$ through history. Later, an infinite series found in Kerala gave many more decimal places.

slides.narration: This table shows some approximations. The Egyptians had about three point one six. Archimedes in Greece trapped pi between two fractions. Aryabhata in India gave sixty-two thousand eight hundred thirty-two over twenty thousand, which is three point one four one six. A very accurate fraction, three hundred fifty-five over one hundred thirteen, is often credited to Zu Chongzhi of China.

slides.heading: Archimedes: trapping pi
slides.body_md: Archimedes drew polygons with $96$ sides inside and outside a circle. Their perimeters gave $\dfrac{223}{71} < \pi < \dfrac{22}{7}$. The gap between the bounds is only $\dfrac{1}{497}$.

visual.alt: A circle of radius 10 units with a regular polygon of 12 sides drawn inside it, with all its corners on the circle. The polygon fills most of the circle, and its area is 300 square units against about 314 for the circle.
visual.caption: A polygon with more and more sides fills the circle better and better.

slides.narration: Archimedes drew regular polygons inside a circle and outside it. The more sides the polygon has, the closer it hugs the circle. With polygons of ninety-six sides he showed that pi is bigger than two hundred twenty-three over seventy-one, and smaller than twenty-two over seven. Those two bounds are only about two thousandths apart.

slides.heading: Quick check: Aryabhata
slides.body_md: Aryabhata gave sixty-two thousand eight hundred thirty-two over twenty thousand for pi. As a decimal, what is it?

slides.heading: Arc length
slides.body_md: An arc of a sector of angle $\theta$ is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circumference: $\ell = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$. Here $r = 9$ cm and $\theta = 100^\circ$. The **perimeter of the sector** is $\ell + 2r$.

visual.alt: A sector with the centre O, two radii OA and OB of 9 centimetres each, and the arc AB between them. The angle AOB at the centre is 100 degrees.
visual.caption: Sector of radius $9$ cm and angle $100^\circ$. With $\pi = 3.14$: arc $= 15.7$ cm, area $= 70.65$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: A sector is cut off by two radii. Its curved edge is an arc. If the angle at the centre is theta degrees, the arc is theta over three hundred sixty of the whole circumference. In the figure the radius is nine centimetres and the angle is one hundred degrees. The perimeter of the sector is the arc plus the two radii.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: circumference and arc
slides.body_md: Find the distance rolled in $100$ turns by a wheel of diameter $70$ cm, and the arc of $100^\circ$ in a circle of radius $9$ cm.
bullets: **Wheel, $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$ —** $C = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 70 = 220$ cm, so $100$ turns cover $22000$ cm $= 220$ m

visual.alt: Table: a wheel of diameter 70 centimetres has circumference 220 centimetres using 22 over 7. A circle of radius 9 centimetres has circumference 56.52 using 3.14. An arc of 100 degrees on it is 100 over 360 of that, which is 15.7 centimetres.
visual.caption: The arc is the fraction $\theta/360$ of the circumference.

slides.narration: For the wheel, the circumference is twenty-two sevenths times seventy, which is two hundred twenty centimetres. In one hundred turns it covers twenty-two thousand centimetres, or two hundred twenty metres. For the circle of radius nine, using three point one four, the circumference is fifty-six point five two, and the arc of one hundred degrees is fifteen point seven centimetres.

slides.heading: Perimeter of a composite figure
slides.body_md: A window is a rectangle with a **semicircle** on top. Its frame is the two sides, the bottom and the curved arc. The dashed diameter is **not** part of the frame.

visual.alt: A window made of a rectangle 56 centimetres wide and 80 centimetres high with a semicircle of radius 28 centimetres on top. The dashed line is the diameter of the semicircle; it is not part of the frame.
visual.caption: Frame: $80 + 56 + 80$ plus the semicircular arc $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 28 = 88$ cm.

slides.narration: Here is a window made of a rectangle with a semicircle on the top. To find the length of the frame, add only the outside edges: the two sides, the bottom, and the curved part. The straight line across the top is inside the window, so it is not part of the frame. The curved part is half a circumference.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the window frame
slides.body_md: A window is $56$ cm wide and $80$ cm high at the sides, with a semicircle of radius $28$ cm on top. Find the length of the frame. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

visual.alt: Table: the frame of the window has two sides of 80 centimetres, a bottom of 56 centimetres and a semicircular arc of 88 centimetres, using 22 over 7. The total is 304 centimetres. The top diameter is not part of the frame.
visual.caption: Perimeter of a composite figure: add only the outside edges.

slides.narration: The two sides and the bottom add up to two hundred sixteen centimetres. The semicircle is half a circle, so its length is pi times the radius, twenty-two sevenths times twenty-eight, which is eighty-eight centimetres. The whole frame is two hundred sixteen plus eighty-eight, which is three hundred four centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: the clock hand
slides.body_md: The tip of a minute hand is seventeen and a half centimetres from the centre. How far does it travel in twelve minutes?

visual.alt: A sector with the centre O, two radii OA and OB of 9 centimetres each, and the arc AB between them. The angle AOB at the centre is 100 degrees.
visual.caption: Sector of radius $9$ cm and angle $100^\circ$. With $\pi = 3.14$: arc $= 15.7$ cm, area $= 70.65$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: Twelve minutes is a fraction of a full turn of the minute hand.

slides.heading: Heron's formula
slides.body_md: A triangle with sides $a$, $b$, $c$ has area $\sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$, where $s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2}$. It needs **no height**. Heron of Alexandria described it in the first century CE.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with AB of 25 centimetres, AC of 29 centimetres and BC of 36 centimetres. The dashed height AF from A to BC is 20 centimetres and makes a right angle with BC.
visual.caption: Heron: $s = 45$, area $= \sqrt{45 \times 20 \times 16 \times 9} = 360$ cm$^2$, the same as $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 36 \times 20$.

slides.narration: Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle when you know only its three sides. First find s, half the perimeter. Then multiply s by s minus a, s minus b and s minus c, and take the square root. You do not need the height. The method is named after Heron of Alexandria, who described it in the first century.

slides.heading: Using Heron's formula
slides.body_md: For the triangle $25$, $29$, $36$ cm the formula agrees with $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$, where the height on the side $36$ is $20$.

visual.alt: Table: for the triangle with sides 25, 29 and 36 centimetres, s is 45 and the differences are 20, 16 and 9. The product 45 times 20 times 16 times 9 is 129600 and its square root is 360 square centimetres, the same as half of 36 times the height 20.
visual.caption: Heron's formula: area $= \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$.

slides.narration: Take a triangle with sides twenty-five, twenty-nine and thirty-six. Half the perimeter is forty-five. The three differences are twenty, sixteen and nine. The product is one hundred twenty-nine thousand six hundred, and its square root is three hundred sixty. The same triangle has a base of thirty-six and a height of twenty, and half of that product is also three hundred sixty.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a plot with a right angle
slides.body_md: A plot has sides $9$ m, $40$ m and $41$ m. Find its area by Heron's formula and check it.
bullets: **Check —** $9^2 + 40^2 = 41^2$, so the angle is a right angle and the area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 40 = 180$

rows: Right angle at the corner of $9$ and $40$

visual.alt: Table: a plot with sides 9, 40 and 41 metres has s equal to 45, differences 36, 5 and 4, and area the square root of 32400, which is 180 square metres. The sides satisfy 81 plus 1600 equals 1681, so the angle is a right angle and half of 9 times 40 is also 180.
visual.caption: Heron's formula agrees with $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.

slides.narration: The semi-perimeter is forty-five. The differences are thirty-six, five and four. The product under the root is thirty-two thousand four hundred, and the root is one hundred eighty. As a check, nine squared plus forty squared is forty-one squared, so the triangle has a right angle, and half of nine times forty is also one hundred eighty square metres.

slides.heading: A median bisects the area
slides.body_md: $D$ is the mid-point of $BC$. The median $AD$ cuts the triangle into $ABD$ and $ADC$ with **equal bases** $BD = DC$ and the **same height**, so their areas are **equal**.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with D the mid-point of BC. The median AD splits the triangle into triangles ABD and ADC. BD and DC are 7 centimetres each, and the dashed height from A to BC is 12 centimetres for both triangles, so each has area 42 square centimetres.
visual.caption: Equal bases $BD = DC = 7$ cm and the same height $12$ cm: each half has area $42$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: A median joins a corner to the mid-point of the opposite side. Look at the two triangles it makes. Their bases are equal, seven centimetres each. Both have the same height from the corner A, twelve centimetres. Since the area is half base times height, the two triangles have equal areas, forty-two square centimetres each.

slides.heading: Why a median bisects the area
slides.body_md: The proof uses only equal bases and a common height.

rows: The height $h$ from $A$ to $BC$ is the same for $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ADC$
Both triangles have their base on the line $BC$

visual.alt: Table: a median AD splits triangle ABC. BD equals DC and the height from A is the same for both triangles, so half base times height gives equal areas. In the figure each is 42 square centimetres and the whole is 84.
visual.caption: A median bisects the area of a triangle.

slides.narration: The proof has four steps. D is the mid-point, so the two bases are equal. The height from A to the line B C is the same for both triangles. Write each area as half base times height. Since the bases are equal and the height is common, the areas are equal. In the figure, forty-two and forty-two make eighty-four.

slides.heading: Quick check: Heron's formula
slides.body_md: A triangular plot has sides nine, ten and seventeen metres. What is its area?

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with AB of 25 centimetres, AC of 29 centimetres and BC of 36 centimetres. The dashed height AF from A to BC is 20 centimetres and makes a right angle with BC.
visual.caption: Heron: $s = 45$, area $= \sqrt{45 \times 20 \times 16 \times 9} = 360$ cm$^2$, the same as $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 36 \times 20$.

slides.narration: Find s first, then the three differences.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Circumference $C = 2\pi r = \pi d$; always state the value of $\pi$ used
Arc length $\ell = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$; perimeter of a sector $= \ell + 2r$
Ancient values of $\pi$: Egypt $\dfrac{256}{81}$, Archimedes $\dfrac{223}{71} < \pi < \dfrac{22}{7}$, Aryabhata $\dfrac{62832}{20000}$
A **median** bisects the area of a triangle: equal bases, same height

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: circumference 2 pi r, arc length theta over 360 times 2 pi r, Heron's formula for the area of a triangle, and a median halves the area.
visual.caption: Four tools of Part 1.

slides.narration: To sum up. The circumference is two pi r, and you must say which value of pi you use. An arc is a fraction of the circumference. People in Egypt, Greece and India each found approximations of pi. Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle from its sides. And a median splits a triangle into two triangles of equal area.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Circle numericals (2–3 marks):** write the formula, the value of $\pi$, then the working and the unit
**Heron (2–3 marks):** find $s$, the three differences, the product, then the root
**Mistake:** forgetting the two radii in the perimeter of a sector
**Mistake:** using $s$ as the perimeter instead of half the perimeter
slides.narration: In circle problems, write the formula, say which value of pi you use, then show the working and give the unit. In Heron problems, find s, then the three differences, then the product and the root. Two common slips are forgetting the two radii in the perimeter of a sector, and using the whole perimeter in place of half of it.

decks.title: Area and Perimeter: Part 2, circles, sectors, composite figures and Brahmagupta's formula
goals: Find the area of a circle, a sector, a segment and a ring
Find areas of simple composite figures
State and use Brahmagupta's formula for a cyclic quadrilateral
Show that Heron's formula is the special case d equal to 0

slides.heading: Tiles, tanks and plots
slides.body_md: A circular design on a square tile, a pond with a path, a plot of land: all need **areas**. The area of a circle of radius $r$ is $\pi r^2$.

visual.alt: A square tile of side 28 centimetres with the largest circle drawn inside it, touching all four sides. The radius of the circle is 14 centimetres. The four corner pieces outside the circle make up the area to be found.
visual.caption: Corner pieces $= 28^2 - \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14^2 = 784 - 616 = 168$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: Think of a round design on a square floor tile, a pond with a path round it, or a plot of land with four sides. To buy paint, tiles or seeds, we need to know areas. In this part we find the area of a circle, parts of a circle, and combined shapes, and then a fine formula for four-sided plots.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **area of a circle** and of a **sector**
Find the area of a **segment** and of a **ring**

visual.alt: Flow of Part 2: the area of a circle, sectors and segments, composite figures and rings, and Brahmagupta's formula for a cyclic quadrilateral with Heron's formula as a special case.
visual.caption: Part 2 road map.

slides.narration: First we find areas of circles, sectors and segments. Then we combine shapes, such as a circle inside a square, and a path around a pond, which is called a ring. Finally we learn a formula found by the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta for the area of a four-sided figure whose corners lie on a circle.

slides.heading: Area of a circle
slides.body_md: Cut a circle into many thin pieces, or fit a polygon with more and more sides inside it. The area of a circle of radius $r$ is $\pi r^2$.

visual.alt: A circle of radius 10 units with a regular polygon of 12 sides drawn inside it, with all its corners on the circle. The polygon fills most of the circle, and its area is 300 square units against about 314 for the circle.
visual.caption: A polygon with more and more sides fills the circle better and better.

slides.narration: A regular polygon drawn inside a circle fills most of the circle. The more sides the polygon has, the closer its area gets to the area of the circle. In the end, we find that the area of a circle of radius r is pi times r squared.

slides.heading: Sector of a circle
slides.body_md: A sector with angle $\theta$ is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circle, so its area is $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$.

visual.alt: A sector with the centre O, two radii OA and OB of 9 centimetres each, and the arc AB between them. The angle AOB at the centre is 100 degrees.
visual.caption: Sector of radius $9$ cm and angle $100^\circ$. With $\pi = 3.14$: arc $= 15.7$ cm, area $= 70.65$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: A sector of angle theta is the fraction theta over three hundred sixty of the whole circle. So its area is that fraction of the area of the circle. In the figure the radius is nine centimetres and the angle is one hundred degrees, so the sector is five eighteenths of the circle.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a sector
slides.body_md: Find the arc, area and perimeter of the sector of radius $9$ cm and angle $100^\circ$. Use $\pi = 3.14$.

visual.alt: Table: a sector of angle 100 degrees is 5 over 18 of the circle. Its arc is 15.7 centimetres, its area is 70.65 square centimetres and its perimeter is 33.7 centimetres, with pi equal to 3.14.
visual.caption: A sector is the fraction $\theta/360$ of the whole circle.

slides.narration: The sector is five eighteenths of the circle. Using three point one four, the circumference is fifty-six point five two and the area is two hundred fifty-four point three four. Five eighteenths of these give an arc of fifteen point seven centimetres and an area of seventy point six five square centimetres. The perimeter adds the two radii, so it is thirty-three point seven centimetres.

slides.heading: Formulas for circles and sectors
slides.body_md: Keep the two families apart: **lengths** use $2\pi r$, **areas** use $\pi r^2$.

visual.alt: Table of formulas with the values for a radius of 9 centimetres and angle 100 degrees: circumference 56.52, circle area 254.34, arc 15.7, sector area 70.65 and sector perimeter 33.7.
visual.caption: Sector formulas: the fraction $\theta/360$ of the circle.

slides.narration: Here are the formulas side by side. Lengths use two pi r: the circumference and the arc. Areas use pi r squared: the circle and the sector. For a sector, multiply by theta over three hundred sixty. The perimeter of a sector is the arc plus the two radii. Do not mix the lengths and the areas.

slides.heading: Quick check: a sector
slides.body_md: A sector has radius nine centimetres and angle one hundred degrees. Using pi as three point one four, what is its area?

visual.alt: A sector with the centre O, two radii OA and OB of 9 centimetres each, and the arc AB between them. The angle AOB at the centre is 100 degrees.
visual.caption: Sector of radius $9$ cm and angle $100^\circ$. With $\pi = 3.14$: arc $= 15.7$ cm, area $= 70.65$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: Take five eighteenths of the area of the circle.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a segment
slides.body_md: A chord $AB$ of a circle of radius $14$ cm subtends a right angle at the centre $O$. Find the area of the minor segment. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

visual.alt: A quarter circle with centre O and radius 14 centimetres. The chord AB is dashed, and the triangle OAB is shaded. The segment is the part of the sector between the chord AB and the arc AB.
visual.caption: Segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle $= 154 - 98 = 56$ cm$^2$ (with $\pi = \tfrac{22}{7}$).

slides.narration: A segment is the part of a sector that is left when we remove the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord. For a quarter circle of radius fourteen, the sector has area one hundred fifty-four, and the right triangle has area ninety-eight. The segment is the difference, fifty-six square centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: corners of a square tile
slides.body_md: The largest circle is cut from a square tile of side $28$ cm. Find the area of the four corner pieces. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

visual.alt: Table: a square tile of side 28 centimetres has area 784. The largest circle inside has radius 14 and area 616 using 22 over 7. The four corner pieces together have area 168 square centimetres.
visual.caption: Composite area: subtract the circle from the square.

slides.narration: The tile is a square of side twenty-eight, so its area is seven hundred eighty-four. The biggest circle inside it has a diameter of twenty-eight, so a radius of fourteen, and an area of six hundred sixteen. The four corner pieces together have the difference, one hundred sixty-eight square centimetres.

slides.heading: A ring
slides.body_md: A path round a pond is a **ring** between two circles with the same centre. Its area is $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2 = \pi (R - r)(R + r)$.

visual.alt: Two circles with the same centre O. The inner circle, a pond, has radius 14 metres. The outer circle is the outer edge of a path of width 3.5 metres, so its radius is 17.5 metres.
visual.caption: A path around a pond: inner radius $14$ m, width $3.5$ m, outer radius $17.5$ m.

slides.narration: A path all the way round a circular pond is a ring between two circles with the same centre. Its area is the area of the big circle minus the area of the small circle. If the big radius is capital R and the small radius is small r, this is pi times R squared minus r squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a path round a pond
slides.body_md: A circular pond of radius $14$ m has a path $3.5$ m wide all round it. Find the area of the path. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
bullets: **Areas —** $616$ m$^2$ for the pond and $962.5$ m$^2$ with the path

visual.alt: Table: a path 3.5 metres wide round a pond of radius 14 metres. The pond has area 616, the pond with the path has area 962.5, so the path has area 346.5 square metres, which also equals 22 over 7 times 3.5 times 31.5.
visual.caption: Area of a ring $= \pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi (R - r)(R + r)$.

slides.narration: The path adds three and a half metres to the radius, so the outer radius is seventeen and a half. The pond has an area of six hundred sixteen, and the pond and path together have an area of nine hundred sixty-two and a half. The path is the difference, three hundred forty-six and a half square metres, and the short method gives the same answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: the path
slides.body_md: Use the same pond, radius fourteen metres, with a path three and a half metres wide. What is the area of the path?

visual.alt: Two circles with the same centre O. The inner circle, a pond, has radius 14 metres. The outer circle is the outer edge of a path of width 3.5 metres, so its radius is 17.5 metres.
visual.caption: A path around a pond: inner radius $14$ m, width $3.5$ m, outer radius $17.5$ m.

slides.narration: Outer circle minus inner circle.

slides.heading: Brahmagupta's formula
slides.body_md: A quadrilateral with all four corners on a circle is **cyclic**. With sides $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and $s = \dfrac{a + b + c + d}{2}$, its area is $\sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$. The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta gave it in $628$ CE.

visual.alt: A circle with a quadrilateral ABCD whose four corners lie on the circle. The sides AB, BC, CD and DA are 7, 24, 20 and 15 centimetres. The dashed diagonal AC is a diameter of 25 centimetres, so the angles at B and D are right angles.
visual.caption: A cyclic quadrilateral with sides $7$, $24$, $20$, $15$ cm: area $234$ cm$^2$ by Brahmagupta's formula.

slides.narration: Here is a quadrilateral with all four corners on a circle, called a cyclic quadrilateral. Its sides are seven, twenty-four, twenty and fifteen. The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta gave a formula for its area, using only the sides. Find s, half the perimeter, multiply the four differences s minus each side, and take the square root.

slides.heading: Checking the formula
slides.body_md: Here the diagonal $25$ cm is a diameter, so the figure splits into two right triangles with areas $84$ and $150$. The formula agrees.

rows: $s - a,\ s - b,\ s - c,\ s - d$

visual.alt: Table: for the cyclic quadrilateral with sides 7, 24, 20 and 15 centimetres, s is 33 and the differences are 26, 9, 13 and 18. The product is 54756 and its square root is 234. Splitting along the diameter into two right triangles gives 84 plus 150, which is also 234.
visual.caption: Brahmagupta's formula checked against a computed cyclic quadrilateral.

slides.narration: Let us test the formula. Half the perimeter is thirty-three. The four differences are twenty-six, nine, thirteen and eighteen. Their product is fifty-four thousand seven hundred fifty-six, and the square root is two hundred thirty-four. Now split the figure along the diameter into two right triangles, with areas eighty-four and one hundred fifty. They add up to two hundred thirty-four as well.

slides.heading: A rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral
slides.body_md: A rectangle $8$ cm by $6$ cm has $s = 14$ and the formula gives $\sqrt{6 \times 8 \times 6 \times 8} = 48$, which is length times width.

visual.alt: A rectangle ABCD, 8 centimetres by 6 centimetres, with all four corners on a circle. The diagonal AC is 10 centimetres and is a diameter of the circle. A rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral.
visual.caption: A rectangle is cyclic: Brahmagupta gives $\sqrt{(14 - 8)(14 - 6)(14 - 8)(14 - 6)} = 48$ cm$^2$.

slides.narration: A rectangle has all four corners on a circle, because its diagonal is a diameter. Take a rectangle eight by six. Half the perimeter is fourteen. The four differences are six, eight, six and eight. The square root of their product is forty-eight, which is exactly length times width. So the formula works for rectangles.

slides.heading: Heron's formula as a special case
slides.body_md: Let one side shrink to $0$: $d = 0$. The quadrilateral becomes a triangle, $s - d$ becomes $s$, and Brahmagupta's formula becomes **Heron's formula**.

visual.alt: Table: with d equal to 0, Brahmagupta's formula uses the factors 17, 9, 8 and 34 for the sides 17, 25 and 26, which are the same four numbers as in Heron's formula, so both give the square root of 41616, which is 204.
visual.caption: Heron's formula is the special case $d = 0$ of Brahmagupta's formula.

slides.narration: Now let one side of the cyclic quadrilateral shrink to nothing. The quadrilateral turns into a triangle. In the formula, s minus d becomes just s, so the four factors are s, and s minus each of the three sides. That is exactly Heron's formula. The table shows the same four numbers giving the same area, two hundred four, for a triangle with sides seventeen, twenty-five and twenty-six.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a cyclic plot
slides.body_md: A cyclic plot has sides $25$ m, $39$ m, $60$ m and $52$ m. Find its area.

visual.alt: Table: a cyclic plot with sides 25, 39, 60 and 52 metres has s equal to 88, differences 63, 49, 28 and 36, product 3111696 and area 1764 square metres.
visual.caption: A cyclic plot of land.

slides.narration: The semi-perimeter is eighty-eight. The four differences are sixty-three, forty-nine, twenty-eight and thirty-six. Multiply them to get three million, one hundred eleven thousand, six hundred ninety-six. The square root is one thousand seven hundred sixty-four, so the plot has an area of one thousand seven hundred sixty-four square metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: Brahmagupta
slides.body_md: A cyclic quadrilateral has sides four, five, seven and ten centimetres. What is its area?

visual.alt: A circle with a quadrilateral ABCD whose four corners lie on the circle. The sides AB, BC, CD and DA are 7, 24, 20 and 15 centimetres. The dashed diagonal AC is a diameter of 25 centimetres, so the angles at B and D are right angles.
visual.caption: A cyclic quadrilateral with sides $7$, $24$, $20$, $15$ cm: area $234$ cm$^2$ by Brahmagupta's formula.

slides.narration: Find s, the four differences, and the square root.

bullets: Circle: area $\pi r^2$; sector: $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$; segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle
Ring: $\pi (R^2 - r^2)$; composite figures: add or subtract parts
Cyclic quadrilateral: $\sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$
With $d = 0$ this is Heron's formula; for a rectangle it gives $ab$

notes.title: Area and Perimeter: chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Perimeter and circumference
sections.body_md:
The **perimeter** of a figure is the length of its boundary. The **circumference** of a circle of radius $r$ is $2\pi r = \pi d$, where $\pi$ is the ratio of the circumference to the diameter. $\pi$ is the same for every circle. Use $\dfrac{22}{7}$ or $3.14$ and **say which**.

For a composite figure, add only the outside edges.

key_terms.definition_md: The ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter.

visual.alt: A circle with a diameter AB of 14 centimetres drawn through the centre O. Walking once round the circle covers 22 sevenths of the diameter, which is 44 centimetres.
visual.caption: Circumference $= \pi d = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = 44$ cm.

visuals.alt: Table of perimeters: a rectangle 2 times length plus width, a square 4 times the side, a triangle the sum of its sides, and a circle 2 pi r, which is pi times the diameter. Examples give 40, 36, 36 and 44 centimetres.
visuals.caption: The distance round a circle is called its circumference. State the value of $\pi$ you use.

visuals.alt: A window made of a rectangle 56 centimetres wide and 80 centimetres high with a semicircle of radius 28 centimetres on top. The dashed line is the diameter of the semicircle; it is not part of the frame.
visuals.caption: Frame: $80 + 56 + 80$ plus the semicircular arc $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 28 = 88$ cm.

visuals.alt: Table: the frame of the window has two sides of 80 centimetres, a bottom of 56 centimetres and a semicircular arc of 88 centimetres, using 22 over 7. The total is 304 centimetres. The top diameter is not part of the frame.
visuals.caption: Perimeter of a composite figure: add only the outside edges.

sections.heading: 2. Approximations of pi
sections.body_md: $\pi = 3.14159265\ldots$ and no fraction equals it exactly. Historical values: ancient Egypt (about $1650$ BCE) $\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right)^2 = \dfrac{256}{81} \approx 3.16$; Archimedes (about $250$ BCE) $\dfrac{223}{71} < \pi < \dfrac{22}{7}$ using polygons of $96$ sides; Aryabhata ($499$ CE) $\dfrac{62832}{20000} = 3.1416$; the fraction $\dfrac{355}{113} \approx 3.14159$ is often credited to Zu Chongzhi of China ($5$th century CE). Later, an infinite series found in Kerala gave many more decimal places.

rows: Area of a circle taken as the area of a square of side $\frac{8}{9}$ of the diameter
Trapped $\pi$ between the perimeters of polygons of $96$ sides
Gave $62832$ as the approximate circumference of a circle of diameter $20000$
A fraction often credited to Zu Chongzhi (China, 5th century CE)
Easy to use; it is also the upper bound of Archimedes

visual.alt: Table of approximations of pi: ancient Egypt about 3.1605, Archimedes between 3.1408 and 3.1429, Aryabhata 3.1416, a fraction 355 over 113 often credited to Zu Chongzhi about 3.14159, and the school value 22 over 7 about 3.1429.
visual.caption: Approximations of $\pi$ through history. Later, an infinite series found in Kerala gave many more decimal places.

visuals.alt: A circle of diameter 9 units and a square of side 8 units, drawn on the same centre. The ancient Egyptian rule says that the two have nearly the same area: the square has area 64 and the circle has area about 63.6.
visuals.caption: A square of side $\tfrac{8}{9}$ of the diameter has area $64$ for a circle of diameter $9$ (area about $63.6$).

visuals.alt: A circle of radius 10 units with a regular polygon of 12 sides drawn inside it, with all its corners on the circle. The polygon fills most of the circle, and its area is 300 square units against about 314 for the circle.
visuals.caption: A polygon with more and more sides fills the circle better and better.

visuals.alt: Table: 223 over 71 is 3.14085, below pi; 22 over 7 is 3.14286, above pi; the gap between the two bounds is 1 over 497, about 0.002.
visuals.caption: Archimedes trapped $\pi$ in a very narrow gap.

sections.heading: 3. Arc length
sections.body_md: An arc of a sector of angle $\theta$ degrees in a circle of radius $r$ has length $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$. The perimeter of the sector is the arc plus $2r$.

key_terms.definition_md: A part of a circle between two points.

visual.alt: A sector with the centre O, two radii OA and OB of 9 centimetres each, and the arc AB between them. The angle AOB at the centre is 100 degrees.
visual.caption: Sector of radius $9$ cm and angle $100^\circ$. With $\pi = 3.14$: arc $= 15.7$ cm, area $= 70.65$ cm$^2$.

visuals.alt: Table: a wheel of diameter 70 centimetres has circumference 220 centimetres using 22 over 7. A circle of radius 9 centimetres has circumference 56.52 using 3.14. An arc of 100 degrees on it is 100 over 360 of that, which is 15.7 centimetres.
visuals.caption: The arc is the fraction $\theta/360$ of the circumference.

sections.heading: 4. Heron's formula; a median bisects the area
sections.body_md:
A triangle with sides $a$, $b$, $c$ and $s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2}$ has area $\sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$ (Heron of Alexandria, first century CE). No height is needed.

A **median** divides a triangle into two triangles with equal bases and the same height, so it **bisects the area**.

key_terms.definition_md: Half the perimeter: s = (a + b + c) / 2.
A segment joining a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with AB of 25 centimetres, AC of 29 centimetres and BC of 36 centimetres. The dashed height AF from A to BC is 20 centimetres and makes a right angle with BC.
visual.caption: Heron: $s = 45$, area $= \sqrt{45 \times 20 \times 16 \times 9} = 360$ cm$^2$, the same as $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 36 \times 20$.

visuals.alt: Table: for the triangle with sides 25, 29 and 36 centimetres, s is 45 and the differences are 20, 16 and 9. The product 45 times 20 times 16 times 9 is 129600 and its square root is 360 square centimetres, the same as half of 36 times the height 20.
visuals.caption: Heron's formula: area $= \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$.

rows: Right angle at the corner of $9$ and $40$

visuals.alt: Table: a plot with sides 9, 40 and 41 metres has s equal to 45, differences 36, 5 and 4, and area the square root of 32400, which is 180 square metres. The sides satisfy 81 plus 1600 equals 1681, so the angle is a right angle and half of 9 times 40 is also 180.
visuals.caption: Heron's formula agrees with $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.

visuals.alt: A triangle ABC with D the mid-point of BC. The median AD splits the triangle into triangles ABD and ADC. BD and DC are 7 centimetres each, and the dashed height from A to BC is 12 centimetres for both triangles, so each has area 42 square centimetres.
visuals.caption: Equal bases $BD = DC = 7$ cm and the same height $12$ cm: each half has area $42$ cm$^2$.

rows: The height $h$ from $A$ to $BC$ is the same for $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ADC$
Both triangles have their base on the line $BC$

visuals.alt: Table: a median AD splits triangle ABC. BD equals DC and the height from A is the same for both triangles, so half base times height gives equal areas. In the figure each is 42 square centimetres and the whole is 84.
visuals.caption: A median bisects the area of a triangle.

sections.heading: 5. Area of circles, sectors, segments and rings
sections.body_md: Circle: $\pi r^2$. Sector of angle $\theta$: $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$. Segment: area of the sector minus area of the triangle formed by the radii and the chord. Ring (path round a circle): $\pi(R^2 - r^2) = \pi(R - r)(R + r)$. For composite figures, add or subtract the areas of the parts.

key_terms.definition_md: The region between a chord and an arc.
The region between two circles with the same centre.

headers: Polygon inside a circle of radius $r$

visual.alt: Table: the area of a regular polygon inside a circle divided by the square of the radius is about 2.598 for 6 sides, 3 for 12 sides, 3.106 for 24 sides and 3.139 for 96 sides. For the circle it is pi, about 3.142.
visual.caption: More sides, better fit: the area of a circle is $\pi r^2$.

visuals.alt: Table of formulas with the values for a radius of 9 centimetres and angle 100 degrees: circumference 56.52, circle area 254.34, arc 15.7, sector area 70.65 and sector perimeter 33.7.
visuals.caption: Sector formulas: the fraction $\theta/360$ of the circle.

visuals.alt: Table: a sector of angle 100 degrees is 5 over 18 of the circle. Its arc is 15.7 centimetres, its area is 70.65 square centimetres and its perimeter is 33.7 centimetres, with pi equal to 3.14.
visuals.caption: A sector is the fraction $\theta/360$ of the whole circle.

visuals.alt: A quarter circle with centre O and radius 14 centimetres. The chord AB is dashed, and the triangle OAB is shaded. The segment is the part of the sector between the chord AB and the arc AB.
visuals.caption: Segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle $= 154 - 98 = 56$ cm$^2$ (with $\pi = \tfrac{22}{7}$).

visuals.alt: Table: for a radius of 14 centimetres and a right angle at the centre, the sector has area 154, the triangle has area 98, and the segment between the chord and the arc has area 56 square centimetres.
visuals.caption: Area of a segment = area of the sector minus area of the triangle.

visuals.alt: A square tile of side 28 centimetres with the largest circle drawn inside it, touching all four sides. The radius of the circle is 14 centimetres. The four corner pieces outside the circle make up the area to be found.
visuals.caption: Corner pieces $= 28^2 - \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14^2 = 784 - 616 = 168$ cm$^2$.

visuals.alt: Table: a square tile of side 28 centimetres has area 784. The largest circle inside has radius 14 and area 616 using 22 over 7. The four corner pieces together have area 168 square centimetres.
visuals.caption: Composite area: subtract the circle from the square.

visuals.alt: Two circles with the same centre O. The inner circle, a pond, has radius 14 metres. The outer circle is the outer edge of a path of width 3.5 metres, so its radius is 17.5 metres.
visuals.caption: A path around a pond: inner radius $14$ m, width $3.5$ m, outer radius $17.5$ m.

visuals.alt: Table: a path 3.5 metres wide round a pond of radius 14 metres. The pond has area 616, the pond with the path has area 962.5, so the path has area 346.5 square metres, which also equals 22 over 7 times 3.5 times 31.5.
visuals.caption: Area of a ring $= \pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi (R - r)(R + r)$.

sections.heading: 6. Brahmagupta's formula
sections.body_md:
A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four corners on a circle. With sides $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and $s = \dfrac{a + b + c + d}{2}$ its area is $\sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$ (Brahmagupta, $628$ CE).

Put $d = 0$: the quadrilateral becomes a triangle and the formula becomes Heron's formula. For a rectangle with sides $a$, $b$, $s = a + b$ and the area is $ab$.

key_terms.definition_md: A quadrilateral whose four corners lie on a circle.

visual.alt: A circle with a quadrilateral ABCD whose four corners lie on the circle. The sides AB, BC, CD and DA are 7, 24, 20 and 15 centimetres. The dashed diagonal AC is a diameter of 25 centimetres, so the angles at B and D are right angles.
visual.caption: A cyclic quadrilateral with sides $7$, $24$, $20$, $15$ cm: area $234$ cm$^2$ by Brahmagupta's formula.

visuals.caption: Brahmagupta's formula checked against a computed cyclic quadrilateral.

visuals.alt: A rectangle ABCD, 8 centimetres by 6 centimetres, with all four corners on a circle. The diagonal AC is 10 centimetres and is a diameter of the circle. A rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral.
visuals.caption: A rectangle is cyclic: Brahmagupta gives $\sqrt{(14 - 8)(14 - 6)(14 - 8)(14 - 6)} = 48$ cm$^2$.

visuals.alt: Table: with d equal to 0, Brahmagupta's formula uses the factors 17, 9, 8 and 34 for the sides 17, 25 and 26, which are the same four numbers as in Heron's formula, so both give the square root of 41616, which is 204.
visuals.caption: Heron's formula is the special case $d = 0$ of Brahmagupta's formula.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Circle numericals (2–3 marks):* formula, value of $\pi$, working, unit.
- *Heron and Brahmagupta (2–3 marks):* the semi-perimeter, the differences, the product, the root.
- *Composite figures (3 marks):* show the parts and add or subtract.

**Common mistakes**
1. Not stating the value of $\pi$.
2. Forgetting the two radii in the perimeter of a sector.
3. Using $s$ as the whole perimeter.
4. Using the diameter where the radius is needed.
5. Using Brahmagupta's formula for a quadrilateral that is not cyclic.

cards.front_md: What were Archimedes' bounds for pi?

cards.front_md: What value of pi did Aryabhata give?

questions.stem_md: Aryabhata gave $\dfrac{62832}{20000}$ as the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter. As a decimal this is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{62832}{20000} = 3.1416$. The value $3.1429$ is $\dfrac{22}{7}$, $3.1605$ is the ancient Egyptian value $\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right)^2$, and $3.1408$ is $\dfrac{223}{71}$, Archimedes' lower bound (all rounded to four places).

questions.stem_md: The tip of the minute hand of a tower clock is $17.5$ cm from the centre of the dial. In $12$ minutes the tip moves along an arc of length (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: The minute hand turns $6^\circ$ every minute, so in $12$ minutes it turns $72^\circ$. Arc length $= \dfrac{72}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 17.5 = \dfrac{1}{5} \times 110 = 22$ cm. The value $110$ cm is the whole circumference.

questions.stem_md: A triangular plot has sides $9$ m, $10$ m and $17$ m. By Heron's formula its area is
questions.solution_md: $s = \dfrac{9 + 10 + 17}{2} = 18$. Area $= \sqrt{18 \times 9 \times 8 \times 1} = \sqrt{1296} = 36$ m$^2$. The value $45$ is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 10$, which is the area only for a right angle between the sides $9$ and $10$.

questions.stem_md: A sector of a circle has radius $9$ cm and angle $100^\circ$. Its area, using $\pi = 3.14$, is
questions.solution_md: Area $= \dfrac{100}{360} \times 3.14 \times 9^2 = \dfrac{5}{18} \times 254.34 = 70.65$ cm$^2$. The value $254.34$ is the whole circle, and $15.7$ is the length of the arc (in cm).

questions.stem_md: A circular pond of radius $14$ m has a path $3.5$ m wide all round it. The area of the path, using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, is
questions.solution_md: The outer radius is $14 + 3.5 = 17.5$ m. Area of the path $= \dfrac{22}{7}(17.5^2 - 14^2) = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 110.25 = 346.5$ m$^2$. The value $616$ is the pond and $962.5$ is the pond with the path.

questions.stem_md: A cyclic quadrilateral has sides $4$ cm, $5$ cm, $7$ cm and $10$ cm. By Brahmagupta's formula its area is
questions.solution_md: $s = \dfrac{4 + 5 + 7 + 10}{2} = 13$. Area $= \sqrt{(13 - 4)(13 - 5)(13 - 7)(13 - 10)} = \sqrt{9 \times 8 \times 6 \times 3} = \sqrt{1296} = 36$ cm$^2$. The value $13$ is $s$, and $1296$ is the number under the root.

questions.stem_md: The ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter

options.text_md: is smaller for a larger circle
is the same for every circle
is larger for a larger circle

questions.solution_md: For every circle the circumference is $\pi$ times the diameter, so the ratio is the same number $\pi$ for all circles. It is not exactly $\dfrac{22}{7}$: $\dfrac{22}{7}$ is only an approximation of $\pi$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these numbers lies between Archimedes' two bounds $\dfrac{223}{71}$ and $\dfrac{22}{7}$ for $\pi$?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{223}{71} \approx 3.14085$ and $\dfrac{22}{7} \approx 3.14286$. Only $3.1416$ lies between them. The number $3.14$ is slightly below the lower bound, $3.1429$ is slightly above the upper bound, and $3.16$ is far above it.

questions.stem_md: The ancient Egyptians took the area of a circle of diameter $d$ to be the area of a square of side $\dfrac{8}{9}d$. This is the same as taking $\pi$ to be
questions.solution_md: Square: $\left(\dfrac{8d}{9}\right)^2 = \dfrac{64}{81}d^2$. Circle: $\pi\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}d^2$. Equating, $\pi = 4 \times \dfrac{64}{81} = \dfrac{256}{81} \approx 3.16$.

questions.stem_md: A rickshaw wheel has diameter $70$ cm. The distance it covers in $100$ complete turns, using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, is
questions.solution_md: One turn covers the circumference $\pi d = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 70 = 220$ cm. In $100$ turns the wheel covers $220 \times 100 = 22000$ cm $= 220$ m. The values $440$ m and $2200$ m come from using $2\pi d$ or from a slip in changing centimetres to metres.

questions.stem_md: The length of an arc of a sector of angle $210^\circ$ in a circle of radius $6$ cm, using $\pi = 3.14$, is
questions.solution_md: Arc length $= \dfrac{210}{360} \times 2 \times 3.14 \times 6 = \dfrac{7}{12} \times 37.68 = 21.98$ cm. The value $37.68$ cm is the whole circumference.

questions.stem_md: In Heron's formula for a triangle with sides $25$ cm, $29$ cm and $36$ cm, the value of $s$ is
questions.solution_md: $s$ is half the perimeter: $s = \dfrac{25 + 29 + 36}{2} = \dfrac{90}{2} = 45$ cm. The value $90$ cm is the whole perimeter.

questions.stem_md: A triangular park has sides $17$ m, $25$ m and $26$ m. Its area is
questions.solution_md: $s = \dfrac{17 + 25 + 26}{2} = 34$, so the area is $\sqrt{34 \times 17 \times 9 \times 8} = \sqrt{41616} = 204$ m$^2$. The value $221$ is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 26 \times 17$, which treats the side $17$ as the height.

questions.stem_md: In triangle $ABC$, $D$ is the mid-point of $BC$ and the area of triangle $ABC$ is $84$ cm$^2$. The area of triangle $ABD$ is
questions.solution_md: The triangles $ABD$ and $ADC$ have equal bases $BD = DC$ and the same height from $A$, so they have equal areas. Each is half of $84$ cm$^2$, that is $42$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A circular table mat has diameter $56$ cm. Its area, using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, is
questions.solution_md: The radius is $56 \div 2 = 28$ cm, so the area is $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 28^2 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 784 = 2464$ cm$^2$. The value $176$ is the circumference, and $9856$ comes from using the diameter as the radius.

questions.stem_md: The largest possible circle is cut from a square sheet of side $28$ cm. The area of the sheet left over, using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, is
questions.solution_md: The largest circle has diameter $28$ cm, so radius $14$ cm and area $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 14^2 = 616$ cm$^2$. The sheet has area $28^2 = 784$ cm$^2$, so $784 - 616 = 168$ cm$^2$ is left. The value $1400$ is $784 + 616$.

questions.stem_md: Putting $d = 0$ in Brahmagupta's formula $\sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$ gives
questions.solution_md: With $d = 0$ the quadrilateral becomes a triangle with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, and $s - d$ becomes $s$. The formula is then $\sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$, which is Heron's formula.

questions.stem_md: A semicircular window has diameter $14$ cm. The perimeter of its frame, including the straight diameter and using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, is
questions.solution_md: The curved part is half of a circumference: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 = 22$ cm. Adding the straight diameter, $22 + 14 = 36$ cm. The value $22$ cm leaves out the diameter, and $44$ cm is a whole circle.

questions.stem_md: The number $\pi$ is the same for every circle.
questions.solution_md: $\pi$ is the ratio of the circumference to the diameter, and this ratio is the same for every circle, large or small. The statement is true.

questions.stem_md: The perimeter of a sector of a circle is equal to the length of its arc.
questions.solution_md: The boundary of a sector also includes the two radii, so the perimeter is the arc plus $2r$. For a quadrant of radius $7$ cm the arc is $11$ cm but the perimeter is $11 + 14 = 25$ cm. The statement is false.

questions.stem_md: Archimedes found the exact value of $\pi$.
questions.solution_md: Archimedes found two fractions, $\dfrac{223}{71}$ and $\dfrac{22}{7}$, with $\pi$ between them. He gave bounds, not the exact value, and $\pi$ cannot be written exactly as a fraction. The statement is false.

questions.solution_md: Heron's formula works for every triangle. For the right-angled triangle with sides $9$, $40$, $41$ it gives $\sqrt{45 \times 36 \times 5 \times 4} = 180$, the same as $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 40$. The statement is true.

Area $= \sqrt{(23 - 5)(23 - 8)(23 - 13)(23 - 20)} = \sqrt{18 \times 15 \times 10 \times 3} = \sqrt{8100} = 90$ m$^2$.

Cost $= 90 \times 40 = \text{Rs } 3600$.

questions.stem_md: (a) State Brahmagupta's formula for the area of a cyclic quadrilateral with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$. (b) Find the area of a cyclic quadrilateral with sides $4$ cm, $12$ cm, $14$ cm and $18$ cm. (c) Put $d = 0$ and use the sides $17$, $25$, $26$ to show that the formula gives Heron's formula and find the area. (d) For a rectangle with sides $a$ and $b$, show that the formula gives $ab$. (e) Check (d) for a rectangle $12$ cm by $5$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Area $= \sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$, where $s = \dfrac{a + b + c + d}{2}$.

**(b)** $s = \dfrac{4 + 12 + 14 + 18}{2} = 24$. Area $= \sqrt{20 \times 12 \times 10 \times 6} = \sqrt{14400} = 120$ cm$^2$.

**(c)** With $d = 0$, $s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2}$ and $s - d = s$, so the formula becomes $\sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$, which is Heron's formula. For $17$, $25$, $26$: $s = 34$ and the area is $\sqrt{34 \times 17 \times 9 \times 8} = \sqrt{41616} = 204$.

**(d)** The sides are $a$, $b$, $a$, $b$, so $s = a + b$. Then $s - a = b$ and $s - b = a$, and the area is $\sqrt{b \times a \times b \times a} = \sqrt{a^2b^2} = ab$.

**(e)** $\sqrt{5 \times 12 \times 5 \times 12} = 60 = 12 \times 5$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Brahmagupta; Heron as d = 0; the rectangle as a special case.

questions.passage_md: A farmer in Ludhiana has a triangular field $ABC$ with $AB = AC = 13$ m and $BC = 24$ m. The point $D$ is the mid-point of $BC$, and the farmer builds a straight channel along $AD$.

children.stem_md: The area of triangle $ABD$ compared with the area of triangle $ABC$ is
children.solution_md: A median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area, because they have equal bases $BD = DC$ and the same height from $A$. So $\triangle ABD$ has half the area of $\triangle ABC$.

children.stem_md: Find the area of the field $ABC$ in square metres, using Heron's formula.
**(i)** Find the area of the part $ABD$ of the field, and say why.

answer.model_answer_md: The median $AD$ bisects the area: $BD = DC$ and the height from $A$ is common. So the area of $ABD$ is $\dfrac{60}{2} = 30$ m$^2$.

children.stem_md: Which formula gives the area of this plot from its four sides?
children.solution_md: The plot is a cyclic quadrilateral with four sides, so Brahmagupta's formula $\sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$ applies. Heron's formula is for triangles.

questions.solution_md: The area of a circle of radius $r$ is $\pi r^2$. The formula $2\pi r$ is the circumference, and $\pi d$ is the same circumference written with the diameter.

questions.stem_md: The length of an arc of a sector of angle $\theta$ degrees in a circle of radius $r$ is
questions.solution_md: The arc is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circumference, so its length is $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$. The formula with $\pi r^2$ is for the area of the sector.

questions.stem_md: In Heron's formula the letter $s$ stands for

options.text_md: half of the perimeter of the triangle

questions.solution_md: In Heron's formula $s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2}$, the semi-perimeter, which is half of the perimeter.

questions.stem_md: Brahmagupta's formula $\sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$ gives the area of
questions.solution_md: Brahmagupta's formula is for a quadrilateral whose four corners lie on a circle, a cyclic quadrilateral. It does not hold for every quadrilateral.

questions.stem_md: A sector of angle $180^\circ$ is a semicircle.
questions.solution_md: A sector of angle $180^\circ$ is $\dfrac{180}{360} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ of the circle, which is a semicircle. The statement is true.

questions.stem_md: Ravi claims that a circular pond of radius $r$ has a surface area of $2\pi r$.
questions.solution_md: $2\pi r$ is the circumference, a length. The area is $\pi r^2$. For $r = 7$ cm and $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$ the circumference is $44$ cm but the area is $154$ cm$^2$. The statement is false.

questions.stem_md: The region between two circles with the same centre is called a ____.
questions.solution_md: The region between two concentric circles is called a ring (an annulus). So the blank is ring.

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between the circumference and the area of a circle of radius $r$. Give the formula for each and the unit of each, for a radius in centimetres.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **circumference** is the length of the boundary, $2\pi r$, measured in cm. The **area** is the space inside the circle, $\pi r^2$, measured in cm$^2$.

For $r = 7$ cm and $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$ they are $44$ cm and $154$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Circumference: length, 2 pi r, cm. Area: space inside, pi r squared, cm squared.
